final_answer:
Antibiotic resistance arises through a process of natural selection. When antibiotics are used, they kill most of the susceptible organisms in a population. However, some individuals may possess genetic traits that allow them to survive the treatment. These traits can be the result of random mutations or other genetic variations. Over time, these surviving organisms reproduce, passing on their resistant traits to their offspring. This leads to an increase in the proportion of resistant individuals in the population.

Overprescription of antibiotics accelerates this process. When antibiotics are used unnecessarily or inappropriately, they expose large numbers of organisms to selective pressure. This pressure favors the survival and proliferation of resistant variants. In environments where antibiotics are frequently used, such as in healthcare or agriculture, the chances of resistant organisms spreading and becoming dominant increase significantly. This creates a cycle where resistance becomes more common and harder to manage.
